To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dietary glycemic index of adolescents is not associated with their body fat or BMI during puberty.
dietary glycemic index or glycemic load, fiber intake, and whole-grain intake do not appear to affect body composition or body mass index in adolescents.
dietary GI, GL and fiber and whole grain intakes in healthy adolescents do not appear relevant to the development in %BF and BMI during puberty.

the role of diet in the etiology of obesity and the metabolic syndrome.

dietary GI, GL and fiber and whole grain intakes in healthy free-living adolescents are not related to the development of body fatness or BMI during puberty, but that this may be different in obese adolescents.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we did not find a relationship between dietary glycemic index and glycemic load with percent body fat and BMI.
dietary GI, GL and fiber and whole grain intake do not appear to influence the concurrent development of %BF and BMI in adolescents.
dietary glycemic index and glycemic load, fiber intake, and whole-grain intake are not relevant to the development in body fatness and body mass index during puberty.

, in the context of a healthy lifestyle, the glycemic load of the diet does not appear to play a major role in the development of body fatness during puberty.
, at least in healthy, free living adolescents, dietary GI, GL and fiber intake do not seem to be relevant to body fat gain during puberty.
